meta.dataset: The Structure of Stand-Up Comedy (Pudding, Feb 2018) — Ali Wong's Baby Cobra

det_01.label: Origin: The Pudding's hand-coded transcript
det_01.content: This dataset was created by The Pudding for a February 2018 visual essay titled 'The Structure of Stand-Up Comedy' by Russell Samora and Matt Daniels. The team began with the closed-caption file from Ali Wong's Netflix special Baby Cobra and then 'individually annotated the entire routine, then collectively reviewed and merged into a single data set,' with assistance from Amber Thomas and Caitlyn Ralph. Two CSV files result: ali-wong--captions.csv (925 caption rows, each with start/stop timestamps, the spoken text, a per-caption laughter duration, and a topic-group ID) and ali-wong--topics.csv (131 rows describing the hierarchical topic structure with levels 1-6 and explicit callback links). The Pudding's last-modified date is 12 February 2018.

det_02.label: Subject: Ali Wong's Baby Cobra (2016)
det_02.content: Baby Cobra is a Netflix stand-up special filmed in September 2015 at the Neptune Theater in Seattle and released on Mother's Day, 8 May 2016. Ali Wong was seven months pregnant during the recording — a fact that becomes a recurring structural element in the routine. The special is roughly an hour long (the dataset's last caption ends at 3,535 seconds, or about 58:55, which matches the special's running time when titles are excluded). Reception was strong: New York Magazine described its release as 'the sort of star-making moment that unites the tastes of the unlikeliest fans,' and Baby Cobra is widely credited with launching Wong from comedy-writer (Fresh Off the Boat) to mainstream comedy star.

det_03.label: Background: what a callback is
det_03.content: A callback is a structural device in stand-up: the comic refers to material established earlier in the same set and recontextualizes it for a new laugh. Callbacks are not simple repetitions — they must work as a fresh joke and reward the audience for having paid attention. Practitioners describe two effects that matter for The Pudding's argument. First, callbacks make a long set feel less like a list and more like a single connected piece of writing. Second, distance matters: a callback that arrives a few seconds later feels like part of the original beat, while a callback that arrives many minutes later operates more like a surprise reveal, because the audience has half-forgotten the seed. In Wong's special, the topics CSV records three explicit callbacks (rows where the `callback` column points back to a prior topic's start time), so the dataset lets us see this technique used at long range.

det_04.label: Why it matters: what the original Pudding piece argued
det_04.content: The original Pudding essay argues that stand-up exists on a spectrum from one-liners (Mitch Hedberg) to fully narrative, structurally interconnected routines, and that Ali Wong's special sits far down the structural end. Their core claim — and the reason this dataset is useful — is that Wong's biggest laugh, the 'laughter climax', does not get its size from the punchline alone. It gets its size because by that moment the audience is holding several earlier topics in their head simultaneously, and the joke ties them together. The dataset lets readers test this claim: each caption row carries a measured laughter duration in seconds, and the topics CSV records when one bit calls back to another. We can therefore line up the moments where structure converges with the moments where the audience laughed hardest.

facts: Stand-up exists on a spectrum from one-liners to narrative-driven comedy.

det_05.label: Interpretive hook: laughter as the only ground truth
det_05.content: Caption-level laughter duration is an unusual quantitative signal. Most analyses of comedy text are about word choice, timing, or rhythm; here the audience's reaction is measured in seconds and attached to the exact line that triggered it. That gives us a direct dependent variable. But two confounds deserve a flag for the analyst. First, laughter is contagious and lagged — the seconds tagged to a caption are partly a reaction to *that* line and partly tail-off from the previous beat. Second, the laughter values are quantized in coarse units (whole and half seconds) by hand, so very small differences should not be over-interpreted. The headline patterns — biggest single laugh, distribution shape, where laughter clusters — are robust to both confounds.

det_06.label: Scope suggestion: what the analyst should hunt for
det_06.content: Given the structure of the data, the most productive analyses are: (1) where exactly the largest laugh sits in the hour and what topic produced it; (2) the shape of the laughter distribution — is comedy mostly small reactions punctuated by occasional spikes, or evenly distributed?; (3) topic depth — how deep does Wong's nesting go, and does deeper nesting correlate with bigger laughs?; (4) the three explicit callbacks — when does each one arrive, how far back does it reach, and how big is the laugh at the moment of convergence?; (5) talk-vs-laugh share — what fraction of the hour is the audience laughing rather than the comic talking? These directly test the Pudding piece's central claim that structure, not punchline, drives the climax.

det_07.label: Benchmark: typical laugh-track and audience reaction durations
det_07.content: For context on the laughter durations recorded in this dataset: standard sitcom laugh tracks tend to insert reactions of around 1.5-3 seconds, and live audience laughter on late-night talk shows generally runs 2-5 seconds for a strong joke. Anything above roughly 6 seconds is unusual — it implies the audience kept laughing through the silence the comic deliberately left. This benchmark is what lets us call a 10-second laugh in the data 'extreme' rather than just 'big': it's well outside the normal range of laughter responses for filmed comedy.
